newsitem.title: USA: Dow roars ahead despite gloomy Q3 earnings outlook.
newsitem.headline: Dow roars ahead despite gloomy Q3 earnings outlook.

text.p: The U.S. stock market roared ahead, despite projections that third-quarter earnings growth for America's largest corporations would be the weakest in five years and technology earnings would be sub-par.

While second-quarter S&P 500 operating earnings rose an unexpectedly strong 10.1 percent due to a hot U.S. economy, a smaller economic tailwind is seen for the third quarter. Industry analysts expect S&P 500 year-over-year operating earnings to rise by only 6.1 percent for the quarter ended September 30, said First Call director of research Chuck Hill.

Small caps will likely outperform, with earnings growth of about 12 percent, said Prudential Securities' director of small cap research Claudia Mott. "Small caps don't have to deal with the negative currency translations" like large caps.

But overall results will likely be negatively impacted by slowing economic growth in the third quarter. Gross domestic product growth for the third quarter is seen at 2.5 percent, down from the second quarter's estimated 4.8 percent pace.
"I'm concerned about my third quarter earnings forecasts," said Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist at UBS Securities.
"The consumer is slowing down, there's no pricing power yet and there's some inventory buildup," she said.
"Interest rates are up and the economy is slowing -- not a good combination for 1997 earnings either."
Hill said S&P earnings were revised down at a faster than usual pace from early May forecasts of 9.8 percent growth.

"That's more decay than normal," Hill said, although he noted most revisions before quarter's end are downward. "It starts out with the fact that analysts are too bullish. Then they tend to overshoot (on downward revisions), so with actual reports there are more positive surprises than negative."

Hill said while the third quarter would be above trendline growth, "it looks like the lowest year-to-year gain in the fifth year of this upward cycle." He said the trendline growth for the "last 20 years plus has been 5.7 percent even with all these double-digit growth rates in the last four years."

Nonetheless, investors continued to push stock prices into the stratosphere amid hopes of no Fed tightening next week. The Dow industrials powered ahead in record territory, up 54 to 5892 Monday afternoon. The S&P 500 surged five to 686, also in all-time high ground. The tech-laden Nasdaq Composite climbed 10 to 1198, still off its record high.
The Russell 2000, which measures smaller cap issues, rose a more modest two to 343. Technology and many small caps were ravished during the July market correction.
The long bond rose 4/32 to yield 6.94 percent. Dudack noted the long bond is still about 100 basis points above the end of 1995.
Joseph Abbott, an assistant vice president at I/B/E/S, provided the following projections for third-quarter earnings growth in various sectors:
-- Natural Gas, up 254 pct amid a rise in natgas prices
-- Trucking, up 93 pct amid dismal year-ago comparisons
-- Autos, up 85 pct
-- Airlines, up 50 pct
-- Home builders, up 37 pct
Abbott said "the highly cyclical companies are really at the bottom," with I/B/E/S projecting:
-- Paper companies, down 56 pct
-- Truck builders, down 46 pct
-- Aluminum/copper cos, down 42 pct
-- Steel, down 16 pct
Technology will be a mixed bag, with even the solid software group showing a slowing in earnings growth.
I/B/E/S said third-quarter software profits are seen rising 18.5 percent and computer earnings by 5.9 percent but semiconductor results are seen tumbling 32 percent.
Abbott said the biotechnology sector is expected to be the only group reporting a loss for the quarter, totaling $41 million -- up 67 percent from the year-ago loss.

David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers, did not expect third-quarter results "to knock down the market as a whole," as some company warnings did for the second quarter. "The test is the next two weeks," with more earnings pre-announcements, he added.

"We already had some pre-announcements but some of those companies are small," he said. Shulman noted earnings warnings from companies including Rubbermaid Inc, Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc, ITT Corp and Procter & Gamble Co. "Kellogg (Co ) shares took it reasonably well, and Digital (Equipment Corp).

Shulman said he expected stocks to be more preoccupied in the near-term by further Mideast tensions and the November elections, with Wall Street fearful that Democrats will retake control of Congress.

Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter, was more optimistic than others on earnings and stock market prospects. He said Dean Witter cut the cash asset allocation in its basic asset portfolio by five percent from 25 percent, raised stocks to 60 percent from 55 percent and left bonds at 20 percent.
"My guess is not only will third quarter earnings be good, but the fourth quarter will be even better after a lousy fourth quarter last year. That reinforces the upward movement in the market."

Canelo added, "The interest rate outlook is much more important than whatever earnings have been -- that'll determine what earnings will be. If it's less threatening, you can't get over-bearish over profits."
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721
